title: Two's Complement: Flip the Bits, Add One
topic: Two's complement — to represent the negative of an N-bit number, invert every bit and add one; the same adder hardware then does subtraction, and the leading bit acts as the sign

beats.narration: How do you write a negative number in a fixed-width register, without a separate minus-sign wire?

elements.content: Four bits, one register — where does the minus sign go?

beats.narration: Start with unsigned: four bits, weights eight, four, two, one. 0 1 0 1 is four plus one, which is five.

elements.content: Row of four bit boxes showing 0101 with weights 8, 4, 2, 1 above
Highlight the two bits set to 1, sum to 5

elements.position: below the row, serif italic large

beats.narration: To negate the number, first flip every bit — 0 1 0 1 becomes 1 0 1 0. Then add one. The plus one ripples through the low bit, landing at 1 0 1 1. That bit pattern is the two's complement of five: it represents minus five.

elements.content: Bit row, each bit flipping individually with a small toggle animation
Mid-step caption: ones' complement (not quite there)
+1 token slides in from the right, ripples through the LSB
Final bit row 1011 with carry shown briefly

beats.narration: Tick a four-bit counter from zero up through fifteen. Read each pattern two ways — the same bits mean a different decimal under signed and unsigned interpretations. After binary 0 1 1 1 — that is plus seven — the next pattern 1 0 0 0 is minus eight in two's complement, and the counter has rolled all the way around.

elements.content: Big bit display, decimal columns to the right: signed and unsigned
Highlight the wrap point between 0111 and 1000 with a rose-coloured tick

beats.narration: Flip the bits, add one. The leading bit becomes the sign — and the same adder hardware now does subtraction for free.

elements.content: subtraction becomes addition with the same hardware
